<reason>A built the only magnitude-tested path to the motion as written: an explicit cost model that survives pessimistic inputs (triple cost, double escalation, still 40%+ collapse), plus baseline-symmetry answers showing B's harms (churn, frustration, governance burden) afflict the human system too. B landed the debate's most original and memorable mechanism — correlated, identical errors at scale versus bounded linear savings — and its rebuttals ("speculation wearing a decimal point," governance as additive cost) genuinely damaged A's arithmetic. But on a motion that is explicitly a comparison of magnitudes, B's refusal to name any flip point or likelihood left its case resting on unquantified tail risk, and A's closing converted that refusal into "unmeasurable and baseline-blind." B's trust-at-the-touchpoint and governance-erosion points stayed live but were never shown to plausibly exceed a recurring 40-70% collapse. Clear but competitive win for A.</reason>
<best_rebuttal>B's Turn-4 rebuttal ("speculation wearing a decimal point," identical-error liability multiplier, governance costs additive on top of the ten-cent line) was the sharpest single hit; the decisive exchange was B's Turn-8 refusal to name a flip-rate, which A's closing turned into the winning frame: an unmeasurable, baseline-symmetric harm cannot outweigh measured recurring savings.</best_rebuttal>
